P1.evidence: Application read back and used as the hook — 'I saw that you already mentioned that you want to go into the next stage of your life. We'll go into that, see what that looks like.' Frame delivered but three-part not four — where you are, where you want to go, whether we fit — with nothing on what is in the way or what he needs. Agreement taken: 'okay?' → 'Yeah, no problem. Perfect.' Open question verbatim: 'what can we potentially help you with?'

P2.evidence: Training week and diet were run well — 'How does it look like at the moment when it comes to your diet?' followed by real probes on the Coke and the eating window, and the training picture built out to 5x/week, one hour, 6:30am, 45 plus 15. Weight came from a good question ('how much do you think that you want to lose and how much are you now?'); age was volunteered and height never asked. The health-conditions check was never run at all — no hereditary question, no medication question, even after the prospect said 'that's when I take my vitamins and the medication that I take.' The injuries question was asked in the right form but then dropped: multiple back operations, nerve damage, injured knees and shoulder injuries came out and the rep summarised it as 'Okay, so, no injuries. Like, you have had injuries in your lifetime, but at the moment, there's not something that flares up.' Nothing on sleep or energy.

P3.evidence: Two genuinely good moves. 'Explain fit to me' forced a specific answer instead of a slogan — the 20 km walk, fitness for a demanding job, a sharp mind. And the reflect-back landed: 'it sounds like you want to get more of an expert base for yourself where you learn about things. Why behind everything. So you can keep on doing it yourself far into the future without potentially injuring yourself' → 'Well, yeah, that would be ideal.' But he never went outside the physical. There was no 'who else does that impact?' on a call where a wife, a son and a one-year-old grandson all appeared — and the grandson later beat the offer in a straight allocation of $500 a month. The richest emotional material on the call, the friends his age who 'sit on their fat' and the line 'if I [go] before them, I'll be deeply disappointed', got a single acknowledgement and was never opened.

P4.evidence: 'Why are we here now?' was asked and answered thinly ('I like to learn new things'). The blocker question was asked properly — 'Do you feel like if you don't have someone that sort of can help you one-on-one with that, it's going to be a little bit harder?' — got an honest no ('I'm pretty disciplined from that point of view'), and the rep correctly re-aimed at travel, which is the real structural constraint. The stick-with-it checks are genuinely not applicable here: this prospect has trained consistently since he was fifteen and has no history of falling off, so 'why didn't it stick' and 'why can't you stick to it on your own' have no referent. That is a script gap, not a rep failure — the playbook has no path for a prospect whose problem is precision rather than consistency.

P5.evidence: The frame was opened and then abandoned. 'Let's say you keep on doing the exact same thing... Where do you think that you would be at in five to 10 years from now?' got a flat refusal to engage — 'You know, but I have no idea. I don't think about that. I kind of do this kind of thing day at a time' — and the rep responded 'That's understandable. That's understandable' and moved to a compounding-interest analogy. Nothing on willing to settle, nothing on why not, no line in the sand. This is the phase that decided the call: the prospect left with zero cost attached to doing nothing, which is exactly the position from which $6,000 loses to £45 a month.

P6.evidence: The belief question ran well in the prospect's own language — 'do you feel like you're going to have the same compounding interest when you're sort of figuring it out all by yourself, or when you actually do it with someone?' → 'I wouldn't be talking if I didn't think that doing it with someone... That be massively beneficial.' But the all-in question was never asked, and the yes he moved forward on was explicitly conditional: 'I've got no problem making an investment in myself, right? But, you know, I have to see.' The script says return to Phase 5 on hesitation; he presented instead.

P11.evidence: Price was presented and a decision sought, so the phase applies. Nothing ran. No payment, and no deposit was even proposed to a prospect who was going to speak to his wife in two days — the exact scenario the manager coaches the deposit for. No Trevor call, no agreement, no welcome sequence.

objection_plays.detail: 'I'll have to think about it' arrived with the price objection. The rep ran the last scripted move first and ran it excellently — the are-you-sure check, framed as permission to say no: 'Is it really something you have to think about? Just be honest with me... Do you feel like you are actually going to think about it or there is already a made decision for you? Like, if it's already a made decision, that's okay.' That produced the truth in one turn: 'when you say six grand, I was like, no, I'm not going to do that.' But nothing before it ran — no 'thinking isn't the problem, deciding is', no 'the way you've been approaching this brought you here', no 'that man you want to be, how does HE decide right now'. Having surfaced the real answer, he had nowhere to take it.

Ran the isolate — 'out of the money aspect, do you feel like, yeah, I do want to do this?' — and explored what the conversation with the wife would look like and what happens on each outcome, which is a reasonable substitute for 'what obstacles might come up'. Missing: 'is she around' (she was reachable, this was a Sunday at home), 'is there any reason she would NOT want you stronger and less in pain', 'is this genuinely needing her input or asking permission to bet on yourself', and the deposit fallback. He conceded the play outright: 'yeah, then I guess, yeah, go, go talk to her about it.'

Never run, and it is the largest miss on the call. The prospect converted the fee into a monthly figure himself and worked in it for ten minutes — '$1,000 a month', 'do I spend another $500 a month on this', 'whether it's $500, $1,000 a month, doesn't make that much difference to me personally'. He was explicitly comparing monthly allocations, not questioning capacity. No 'you're not in a SHOULD I place, you're in a HOW place', no 'most clients pay upfront, but for some we break it up', no financial picture, no plan of any kind. A prospect who had already done the instalment arithmetic for the rep was never offered instalments.

The controlling objection was value against a cheaper alternative that genuinely works — a £45/month gym, free routines from Facebook including Trevor's own, and fifty years of self-directed training that has produced measurable progress. 'What is that going to bring me in six months that I can't do myself?' The playbook already records this as a known gap from the Badrane Hriouch call and it has not been filled. The rep answered with a compounding-interest analogy the prospect agreed with in principle and then priced out anyway, because agreement in principle is not a delta.

notes: Best objection work in the batch — the permission-to-say-no move got a hedge fund manager to state his real position in one turn, which almost nobody does. It was wasted because the two phases that create room to use it never ran: no consequence frame, so inaction cost him nothing, and no money play, so a man who had already reduced the fee to $500-$1,000 a month in his own head was never offered a structure. Two things to fix, in order: finish Phase 5 when a prospect deflects with 'I don't think about that' — that deflection is the objection — and treat a prospect who talks in monthly numbers as an open-wallet trigger even when he clearly has the cash.
